steps.stem: Artificial organs, such as mechanical hearts and implanted kidney devices, are judged by physicians not in relation to the devices that came before them but in relation to the living organ, which remains the model they are meant to match. This sets them apart from inventions in many other fields, whose novelty was expressed in the name they were given when they first appeared: the radio, for example, was at first known as "the wireless telegraph." Which of the following examples could best replace the example at the end of the paragraph?
choices: Calling the electric refrigerator "an icebox without ice"
Calling a mechanical calculator "a clerk without a pencil"
Calling a submarine "an iron fish"
Calling a wind-up watch "a watch without a battery"
explanation: Like the wireless telegraph, the refrigerator is named after the earlier device it replaced, minus the element that defined that device. (2) and (3) measure the machine against a living model (a person, a fish), which is the contrast the paragraph draws, and a fish is not an earlier device that the submarine replaced; (4) names the older device after a feature of the newer one.

steps.stem: A hotel wanted to stop guests from staying in their rooms past the official check-out time of noon, so the manager announced that guests would be charged a fee for every hour they stayed beyond noon. To the manager's surprise, the number of guests who checked out late rose sharply: many guests, it turned out, were glad to keep their rooms longer, as long as they could pay for it. Which of the following cases is most similar to the case described?
choices: A baker saw that demand for his whole-wheat bread had grown, so he raised its price; to his surprise, he went on selling just as many loaves as before

A magazine stopped including its free travel booklet, and a separate travel magazine began to be sold at almost the same price as the original magazine; to the publisher's surprise, many readers stopped buying the original magazine and bought the travel magazine instead

A city's museums used to let visitors who arrived without booking a time slot enter anyway if there was room; to reduce such visits, the city began charging these visitors a high surcharge; to its surprise, the number of visitors arriving without a booking rose
After a long dispute, a company's management agreed to give its employees an extra day off every month; to its surprise, both output and profits grew
explanation: As at the hotel, a charge meant to deter a tolerated lapse turned it into a service people were willing to buy, and the lapse grew. (1) is a price rise that did not cut demand, (2) is readers switching to a new product, and (4) is a benefit that paid off.

steps.stem: Noga: "I have noticed that whenever Eitan's grades fall, his private tutor has stopped coming to see him. Evidently she loses patience with him when he stops making an effort, and so she gives up on him each time his grades drop." Tami: "Your reasoning is about as sound as the claim that opening umbrellas is what makes it rain." What does Tami mean?
choices: Had Eitan's tutor kept coming, his grades would have fallen even further
Eitan lets his grades fall because he wants his tutor to stop coming
Eitan's grades fall because his tutor stops coming to see him
Eitan's tutor is wrong to give up on him just when he needs her most
explanation: Umbrellas open because it rains, not the other way round: Tami says Noga has reversed cause and effect. (1) adds a "what if", (2) adds a motive, and (4) adds a moral judgment.

steps.stem: Ofer, raising his voice so loudly that the whole office could hear him: "Dana, I was told that you shouted at the new intern this morning! I can hardly believe it. Surely you know that shouting at people never gets anything done." Dana: "If you stop for a moment and listen to yourself, you will see that it is like ____." Which of the following best completes Dana's words?
choices: refusing to lend your neighbor a ladder only because he once refused to lend you his
writing a long, rambling letter to a newspaper to complain that people no longer express themselves briefly
going out to water your garden in the middle of a heavy rainstorm so that the plants will not dry out
complaining that a pickpocket took advantage of the fact that you left your wallet sticking out of your pocket
explanation: Ofer shouts in order to say that shouting is wrong, so his act undermines his own message, like a rambling letter demanding brevity. (1) is retaliation, (3) is a pointless act, and (4) shifts the blame for one's own carelessness.

steps.stem: In a conversation between Maya and Itai, Maya made a remark, and Itai responded: "You sound like someone who decides how good a restaurant's food is by looking at the shape of its plates." Which of the following is most likely to be what Maya said?
choices: "I tried on several pairs of running shoes and bought the most comfortable pair, even though it was expensive."
"The acting in Varden's new play is so wooden that I left at the intermission."
"The coffee at the corner café is too bitter for me – I won't go back there."
"Attorney Amir must be an outstanding lawyer – his office is in the most luxurious tower in the city."
explanation: Itai says Maya judges the main thing by an incidental detail, as in judging a lawyer by his office building. (1), (2) and (3) each judge the thing itself: comfort, acting, taste.

steps.stem: Lior told Boaz that he had ordered a rare cookbook from a shop overseas and would have to wait two months for it to arrive. Boaz replied: "What you are doing is like swimming across a river while there is a bridge just a few steps away. The city library has had a copy of that very book on its shelves for years." In his reply, Boaz compares -
choices: the copy in the city library to the bridge
ordering the book from overseas to the river
the cookbook to the bridge
the copy ordered from overseas to swimming across the river
explanation: The bridge is the easy way to the same place: the library copy. Ordering from overseas is the swimming, not the river (2); the book is what lies on the other side, not the bridge (3); the ordered copy is the goal, not the effort of getting there (4).

steps.title: Parables and comparisons: what they ask
steps.intro: Name the question type, then work the way that type needs.

head: Question type
Typical wording
How to work
rows: Which example could replace… · explain in a similar way
Take the exact logic of the example; keep two, then compare precisely
Break the case into parts; match part by part
What does X mean? · What does X think?
Understand the parable, then translate it back to the conversation
Understand twice: the words, and every parable in the choices
What did X say / what was the context?
A parable answers something said, done or planned
In their reply, X compares ___ to -
Map each element of the parable to the real case

tips: Chicken and egg: check whether someone swapped cause and effect.
A parable is often a polite way of saying "that was a bit silly".
A true or sensible-sounding choice is not enough: it has to work the same way.

steps.stem: For several years now "Orbit," the country's leading publishing house, has been offering contracts to the most talented first-time authors who approach the smaller publishers. Few of these authors' books ever appear: Orbit has more than enough titles of its own, but the small publishers, left without new talent, are losing readers from year to year. Which of the following business practices most resembles Orbit's strategy?
choices: A chain of bakeries acquires the independent bakeries in every neighborhood it moves into, and closes them down
A shoe manufacturer orders the soles for its shoes from a competing manufacturer, so that the competitor will come to rely on the orders and avoid price wars
A furniture maker buys most of the shares of the sawmill that supplies its timber, in order to pay less for the wood
A winery buys the entire harvest of the region's best vineyard, much more than it can use, so that rival wineries must make their wine from inferior grapes
explanation: Orbit acquires what it does not need so that its rivals will lack it; only the winery buys more than it can use in order to deprive its competitors. (1) removes the competitors themselves rather than a resource they need, (2) makes a rival dependent, and (3) is about the buyer's own costs.

steps.stem: Gal and Tamar visited a weekly market held in a hill village and learned that the cheeses sold there, all made by cheesemakers from the village itself, are among the finest in the country. Gal: "I suppose the market is what made them so good – the steady stream of buyers has allowed the cheesemakers to perfect their craft." Tamar: "Your supposition is like supposing that sitting in the front row of a classroom makes people nearsighted." Which of the following claims best expresses what Tamar meant?
choices: Fine cheeses are made in many villages, and there is no reason to look for a special explanation of their quality in this one
The cheeses are fine because they are made from the milk of a rare breed of goat that is raised only in these hills
The market is held in the village precisely because its cheesemakers were already known for their fine cheeses
The market protects the cheesemakers from competition with factory cheese, which has driven cheesemakers out of business elsewhere
explanation: Nearsighted people choose the front row; the front row does not cause nearsightedness. Likewise the good cheesemakers drew the market, not the reverse. (1) denies that any explanation is needed, and (2) and (4) offer other explanations of quality instead of reversing Gal's cause and effect.

steps.stem: Amir told Dafna about a task he had been given in the first week of a course in website design. Dafna's response was: "That is like asking a tailor to sew on the buttons before the cloth has been cut." Which of the following is most likely to be the task Amir told Dafna about?
choices: To choose the fonts and colors for the pages of a website whose structure he would plan only later in the course
To look through websites that the class would analyze in the final weeks of the course
To open a folder for saving the drafts he would submit at the end of the course
To describe the kind of website he hoped to be able to build after the course
explanation: Buttons need cut cloth, and page colors need a planned structure: the finishing touch comes before the thing it depends on. (2) is early preparation, (3) is sensible organization, and (4) asks for a wish, not a product.

steps.stem: Yonatan, who works from home as a translator, needs a new printer and has narrowed his choice to two models: an expensive one whose ink cartridges are cheap, and a cheap one whose cartridges cost a great deal. A colleague advised him to buy the expensive model, saying that, given how much he prints, the savings on cartridges would cover the difference in price within a few months. Which of the following pieces of advice rests on reasoning most similar to the colleague's?
choices: A runner is advised to train on hills rather than on flat roads, since the extra effort will be repaid by faster times in races
A couple is advised to hold their wedding in the spring rather than in the summer, since the weather is milder then
A commuter who takes the train every day is advised to buy an annual pass rather than a ticket each morning, since a year of daily tickets would cost far more than the pass
A hiker is advised to take a smaller tent, since the lighter load will let her cover more ground each day
explanation: In both cases a larger payment now is set against a recurring cost that soon exceeds it. (1) trades effort for results, not money for money over time; (2) and (4) weigh qualities, not costs.

steps.stem: After burglars broke into Mrs. Shavit's apartment and took all her jewelry, her son suggested that she install a safe in her bedroom closet. She replied: "If I did that, I would be like a shepherd who builds a pen once the wolves have carried off the whole flock." Which of the following best expresses what Mrs. Shavit meant?
choices: A safe does offer protection, but its price is out of proportion to the value of what it would guard
The jewelry had been kept in a safe, and the burglary proved that safes are of no use
There is no point in a safe, since burglars who break into an apartment usually know how to open a safe as well
A safe would have been worth installing before the burglary, but now that the jewelry is gone there is nothing left for it to protect
explanation: The pen built after the flock is gone is a precaution taken once the loss it should have prevented has already occurred. (1) makes the objection one of cost, (2) invents an earlier safe, and (3) claims safes do not work, which the image does not say.

steps.stem: Dalia told her friends: "Last week a young woman in my building asked me to help her carry a crib up the stairs, and I said I was in a hurry, as I usually do. That evening my car would not start in the parking lot. I asked three neighbors who were passing to help me push it, and each of them had some excuse, until that same young woman came down and pushed the car with me until the engine started. If not for her, I would have been stuck there all night." Which of the following is least suited to be the moral of Dalia's story?
choices: Whoever refuses to help others today may find that tomorrow they are the ones who need help
Sometimes the only person willing to help is the one who was refused help
Whoever has turned away someone in need has no right to accept that person's help later on
Whoever does not lend others a hand should not be surprised when others do not lend theirs
explanation: Dalia accepted the young woman's help, and the story presents that help as its point, not as something she should have refused. (1), (2) and (4) each draw a lesson that the events support.

steps.stem: Ronit and Hagai were waiting outside an electronics store for Alon, Hagai's son, who had gone in more than an hour earlier. Ronit: "Aren't you afraid that Alon will come out having spent a fortune?" Hagai: "No one posts a guard over a field of thistles." In his reply, Hagai compares -
choices: Alon's spending to the thistles
the time Alon has spent in the store to the field of thistles
himself to the guard
the goods in the store to the thistles
explanation: No one guards thistles because no one wants them; in Hagai's view nothing in the store is worth Alon's money. (1) and (2) turn the thistles into something about Alon's behavior, and (3) puts Hagai in the guard's place, although the point is that no guard is needed.

steps.stem: The caterpillar of a certain species of butterfly gives off a scent resembling that of the larvae of a particular kind of ant. The ants, taking it for one of their own young, carry it into their nest, where it lives among their brood and feeds on the ants' larvae. Which of the following human behaviors most resembles the behavior of this caterpillar?
choices: A man presented forged references in order to be hired as a restaurant's head chef, and once hired persuaded the owner to dismiss the cook who had held the post for years
A woman lent her neighbor a lawnmower, and when he kept putting off returning it she went into his yard and took it back herself
A man found a set of keys in the stairwell and, although he knew that his neighbor had lost such keys there that morning, kept them
A cyclist who rode on the sidewalk told the inspector who stopped him that the bicycle lane was closed, and refused to pay the fine
explanation: The caterpillar uses deception to gain a place it has no right to and then does away with those whose place it is; the forged references and the ousted cook repeat both steps. (2) recovers one's own property, (3) is a failure to return property, and (4) is a lie that displaces no one.

steps.stem: Yuval's teenage son was repainting the walls of his room, and drops of paint were falling on the floor. When Yuval was asked why he was not wiping up the drops, he said: "No one mops the deck while the waves are still breaking over it." In his words, Yuval compares -
choices: wiping up the drops to the waves
the painting of the room to the waves
the drops of paint to mopping the deck
the painting of the room to mopping the deck
explanation: Mopping while the waves still break is wiping up while the painting goes on: the painting is the waves, and wiping is the mopping. (1) and (3) cross the pairs, and (4) puts the painting on the wrong side.

steps.stem: A company that sells bottled mineral water decided to add to its labels, in large letters, the words "Contains no fat." The words were meant as a gimmick, since no water contains any fat, and the company assumed that consumers, who are well aware of this, would pay them little attention. Yet in the months that followed, the company's sales rose markedly, and a survey found that many buyers had chosen its water because of the new label. Which of the following cases most resembles the case described?
choices: A woman chose to buy her washing machine at a certain store because it advertised that its machines come "with free delivery," although she knew that every store in the city delivers washing machines free of charge
A man whose doctor had advised him to eat more fish stopped buying fish after reading a report on mercury in fish, although he knew that the fish he usually bought is of a kind low in mercury
A woman who heard that a flu outbreak had struck a city in another country postponed a visit to a nearby city, although she knew that the outbreak had not spread beyond the first city
A man checked the brakes of a car he had rented, although the rental company had assured him that all its cars are inspected before every rental
explanation: A label that presents something ordinary as special drives the choice, although the buyer knows it is nothing special. In (2), (3) and (4) the caution responds to a risk the person believes might be real.

steps.stem: Yossi, an archive clerk, began coming to work in a bow tie, and the change became the talk of the building. Asked why a tie had caused such a stir, he said: "On a pond where no wind blows, a single falling leaf makes waves." Which of the following best reflects Yossi's meaning?
choices: In a workplace where people like to gossip about one another, any change becomes a subject of conversation
Yossi is a flamboyant person, and so even a small change in him draws attention
Where things hardly ever change, even a minor change such as a new tie attracts attention
Yossi usually avoids changing the way he dresses, and so his colleagues noticed
explanation: The still pond is the archive, where nothing changes, and the leaf is the small change. (1) makes gossip the cause, and (2) and (4) locate the cause in Yossi rather than in his surroundings.

steps.stem: The Tzuriel curve, a sharp bend on a mountain road, is known among drivers as one of the most dangerous spots in the region. The records of the traffic police, however, show that fewer accidents occur at the curve than on the straight stretches of the same road. The police explain this by the curve's reputation: drivers who believe it is dangerous slow down and take extra care as they approach it. Which of the following phenomena is most similar to the phenomenon described?
choices: Riders who are new to horseback riding fall far more often than experienced riders
Speakers who are afraid of forgetting their lines rehearse them so anxiously that they forget them on stage
Installing lights along a dark footpath reduces the number of people who fall on it at night
Hikers who fear getting lost on an unfamiliar trail get lost less often, since they study the map more carefully before setting out
explanation: Fear of a bad outcome leads to precautions that prevent it. (2) is the reverse, fear bringing about what is feared; (1) and (3) involve no belief at all.

steps.stem: At a literary conference, a novelist complained that critics had read into her latest book a political message she had never intended. One of the critics answered her: "A writer is like a gardener who plants a fruit tree: the gardener chooses the seed, the soil and the spot, and tends the tree as it grows, but once the fruit has ripened, it is not the gardener but whoever eats it who decides how it tastes." Which of the following messages did the critic wish to convey?
choices: The novelist indeed wrote the book, but determining its meaning is the task of its readers and not of its author
The novelist may write whatever she pleases, but critics need not review a book they consider poor
Even a reader who knows the book thoroughly cannot thereby discover what its author intended
Even if the novelist intended a particular message when she wrote the book, she may later come to read it differently
explanation: Planting is writing and eating is reading, and the gardener has no say over the taste. (2) lets critics ignore the book, and (3) and (4) concern the author's intentions, which the parable sets aside.

steps.stem: A family was trying to sell its apartment. Since every buyer who came to see it offered less than the family was asking, they decided to advertise it again, hoping that new buyers would offer more. Their real-estate agent objected: "That is like casting the same bait again and again into a pond where the fish will not bite, instead of changing the bait." Which of the following best expresses the agent's meaning?
choices: She thinks that the buyers who offered the lower prices are the most serious buyers
She thinks that the family should lower the price it is asking
She thinks that if the apartment is advertised again, buyers will offer even less
She thinks that the buyers who have already come can be persuaded to raise their offers
explanation: The bait is the asking price, and changing it means lowering the price. (3) is a prediction, and (1) and (4) are about the buyers rather than the step the family should take.

steps.stem: Ruthie: "The way to rescue the orchestra's budget is to cut costs – starting with the first violinists, who are the best-paid musicians in the orchestra." Nimrod: "I suppose you would also advise the captain of a leaking ship to throw the pumps overboard to lighten the load!" Which of the following claims best expresses Nimrod's intention?
choices: The orchestra's other expenses are much larger than the first violinists' salaries
Audiences will go on buying tickets only if the orchestra's leading violinists go on playing in it
The orchestra should hire more musicians rather than fewer
The first violinists will find positions in other orchestras, and the orchestra will not be able to bring them back
explanation: The pumps are what keeps the ship afloat, and the violinists are what keeps the orchestra alive: the saving destroys what it is meant to save. (1), (3) and (4) are objections the image does not make.

steps.stem: Nurit: "Should it be proven beyond doubt that Halperin wrote the manuscript, I would still deny it, for I am certain he did not." Which of the following contradictions most resembles the contradiction in Nurit's words?
choices: "It has indeed been shown that the comet will pass close to the earth, but I cannot tell whether it will pass close, since this has not yet been shown"
"Even if it turns out that most critics admire the film, I shall go on watching it, since I do not enjoy it"
"Many restaurants are indeed overpriced, but some must be reasonably priced, since I have eaten at few overpriced ones"
"Even if it is shown that most cyclists are thin, I will not accept that many cyclists are heavy, since most thin people are cyclists"
explanation: Nurit grants a proof and then denies its conclusion on the strength of the very claim the proof refutes; (1) has the same shape (shown / not shown). (2) is not a contradiction, and (3) and (4) are faulty inferences of other kinds.

steps.stem: Some argue that in order to understand a person's character we should examine their recent experiences and not their early childhood. A psychologist disagreed and illustrated her position with an analogy: "What would we think of a gardener who, noting that the lamp on their porch is far closer to their plants than the sun, concluded that the lamp does much more to make them grow than the sun does?" In her words, the psychologist compares -
choices: early childhood to the plants
recent experiences to the porch lamp
early childhood to the porch lamp
recent experiences to the sun
explanation: The lamp is near but has little influence, like recent experiences; the sun is far but decisive, like early childhood. (3) and (4) swap the two, and (1) makes childhood the thing influenced.

steps.stem: The proportion of residents over the age of seventy in the town of Givat Oren is higher than in any other town in the country. Hadas concluded that something in the town's way of life lengthens its residents' lives. Uri replied: "Your words are exactly like the claim that a restaurant's popularity is determined by the number of cars parked outside it. ____." Which of the following best completes Uri's words?
choices: For Givat Oren has the country's largest and best-equipped homes for the elderly, and every year many elderly people from other towns move there to spend their later years
For it is well known that clean mountain air lengthens life, and since Givat Oren lies higher than any other town in the country, its air is the cleanest
For few children are born in Givat Oren, and when the number of young people in a town is small, the proportion of its elderly residents is naturally higher
For the population of Givat Oren is the smallest in the country, and in so small a population a handful of long-lived residents is enough to raise the proportion markedly
explanation: Cars gather where a restaurant is already popular, and the elderly gather where the town already serves them: the arrow runs from old age to the town. (2) supports Hadas, and (3) and (4) point to errors of other kinds.

steps.stem: Gili: "I've been taking guitar lessons for three weeks now and I still can't play a single song from start to finish, so I'm thinking of quitting." Ido: "You remind me of the fall I planted tulip bulbs and dug one up a week later, grumbling that nothing was growing. That spring, after I had left them alone, as the gardener had told me to, the whole bed was in bloom." What corresponds, in Gili's case, to Ido's digging up the bulb?
choices: Gili's thought of quitting
The songs Gili hopes to be able to play
Gili's first guitar lesson
Gili's attempt, after only three weeks, to play a whole song
explanation: Digging up the bulb is the premature check. (1) corresponds to Ido's grumbling, (2) to the tulips in bloom, and (3) to the planting.

steps.stem: In a conversation between Adi and Ronen, Adi said: "I know that feeling – the one night you lock your bicycle with two chains is the night no one comes near it." Which of the following statements is most likely to be the one of Ronen's to which Adi was responding?
choices: "I trained for months for the marathon, and on the morning of the race it was canceled because of a heat wave."
"For once I backed up all my files before a trip, and this time, of all times, my laptop worked perfectly."
"My car broke down on the day of my job interview, after running for three years without a single problem."
"I baked my neighbor a cake for her birthday, and it turned out that she had just started a strict diet."
explanation: The pattern is a precaution taken for once, followed by the absence of the trouble it guarded against. (3) is the reverse, trouble arriving when unprepared, and (1) and (4) are disappointments of other kinds.

steps.stem: Before you is an argument: "Car thieves are drawn to expensive cars; therefore, if I drive a cheap car, my car will not be stolen." Which of the following arguments most resembles this argument in its logical structure?
choices: Walking is not a dangerous activity; therefore, if I walk, I shall not be injured
Wasps are drawn to sweet drinks; therefore, if I drink a sweet drink outdoors, I shall attract wasps
Employers prefer candidates with a university degree; therefore, if I do not complete my degree, I shall not find a job
Pollen causes sneezing; therefore, if I do not sneeze, I shall not be able to go into the garden
explanation: A single attraction is treated as the only route to an outcome, so that removing it is taken to rule the outcome out. (1) and (4) are faulty inferences of other kinds, and (2) is not this fallacy at all.

steps.stem: Everyone will agree that a person with a hundred thousand hairs on their head is not bald, whereas a person with none, or with only a handful, is. Everyone will also agree that pulling out a single hair from a head that is not bald does not make it bald. If so, when we pull out hair after hair, at what point exactly does the head become bald? Which of the following difficulties is most similar to the one described?
choices: Since a runner's time is recorded only at the finish line, one cannot know during the race whether the runner is on course for a record
Although there is a temperature at which everyone agrees that water is hot, and one at which everyone agrees it is not, no one can name the degree at which it becomes hot
Since people differ in how much noise they can bear, there is no volume at which one can say that a party has become too loud for everyone
Since a tree's growth depends on rainfall that cannot be foreseen, one cannot say how tall a young tree will be in twenty years
explanation: Clear cases at both ends and no point at which one turns into the other. (3) is disagreement between people, and (1) and (4) are lack of information.

steps.stem: Psychologists report that people readily admit that they have changed a great deal over the past decade, yet believe that they will change little in the decade ahead, as though the person they are today were the final version. Which of the following examples best illustrates this phenomenon?
choices: A woman who knows that she no longer holds the political views she held as a student expects to hold her present views for the rest of her life
A man who knows that he still has the same friends he had in school expects to drift apart from some of them in the future
A woman who knows that she is more patient today than she was in her youth expects to become more patient still in old age
A man who knows that he now prefers quieter vacations than he did in his youth thinks that in the future he will again prefer lively ones
explanation: Change is acknowledged in the past and denied for the future. (2), (3) and (4) all expect further change.

steps.stem: At a meeting of a school's teaching staff on ways to reduce the use of phones during lessons, Mr. Ashkenazi said to Ms. Peleg: "You propose to leave a child alone with a jar of candy and ask them not to touch it, when the real way to keep them from eating it is to put the jar on a shelf they cannot reach." What could have been the context in which these words were said?
choices: Peleg proposed that a pupil caught using a phone for the first time be punished more severely than at present, and Ashkenazi argued that the punishment should grow with each further offense
Peleg proposed teaching the pupils about the harm of excessive phone use, and Ashkenazi argued that the time should go instead to making the lessons more engaging
Peleg proposed a rule forbidding pupils to use their phones during lessons, and Ashkenazi proposed that pupils hand in their phones at the classroom door when a lesson begins
Peleg proposed stricter rules against using phones in lessons, and Ashkenazi argued that it is better to enforce the rules that already exist
explanation: Asking the child not to eat is a rule that relies on restraint; the jar out of reach is a phone that is not there to use. (1), (2) and (4) do not set a demand for restraint against removing the temptation.

steps.stem: Tamar's company is launching a product in Japan next month, and she is unsure whether to rely on a local marketing firm or to study the Japanese market herself before the launch. She asked her colleagues Avi and Rina for advice. Avi said: "Better to learn to sew than to keep paying the tailor." Rina said: "But the night before the wedding is no time to take up sewing." Which of the following statements about Avi and Rina is not correct?
choices: Avi argues that relying on a marketing firm would solve Tamar's problem only once
Rina argues that relying on a marketing firm would provide an immediate solution
Both Avi and Rina compare studying the market to learning to sew
Rina disagrees with the view that, in principle, knowing the market oneself is better than relying on a firm
explanation: Rina's "But" grants Avi's principle and objects only to the timing. (1), (2) and (3) each read the images correctly.

steps.stem: The mayor of Beit Shalem decided to stop publishing the city's yearly survey of residents' satisfaction with municipal services. A council member told him: "You are like a driver who tapes over the fuel gauge because it shows that the tank is almost empty." Which of the following is most likely to be the reason for the mayor's decision?
choices: The survey is not prepared efficiently
The city can no longer afford the cost of the survey
The latest survey showed that most residents are dissatisfied with the city's services
The survey causes residents to complain about the city's services
explanation: The gauge only reports the empty tank, as the survey only reports the residents' dissatisfaction. (4) makes the survey the cause of the problem, and (1) and (2) are reasons the image does not touch.

steps.stem: Of Ms. Barak, who manages the most successful branch of a nationwide bank, it is often said: "She is like the wheel of a water mill – it would not turn at all without the stream." Which of the following interpretations is least suited to this saying?
choices: Ms. Barak's branch succeeds only thanks to the unusually skilled staff who work under her
The procedures Ms. Barak applies at the branch were all designed by her predecessor, a celebrated manager
The bank enjoys an excellent reputation, and Ms. Barak's branch benefits from it without any merit of her own

explanation: The mill wheel moves only by a force that comes from outside it; in (1), (2) and (3) Ms. Barak's success comes from someone or something else. In (4) the ability is her own and is merely credited too widely.
